subject: Agriculture
title: Crop Water Footprint
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Crop Water Footprint.

hook.text: A single almond takes about 12 liters of water to grow. A kilogram of beef needs 15,000.

buildup.text: Water footprint measures total water used across the entire supply chain—from seed to supermarket.

discovery.text: Most farm water is 'green water'—rainfall. But irrigated crops use 'blue water' from rivers and aquifers.

twist.text: Exporting water-intensive crops from dry regions is like exporting water itself. Virtual water flows with trade.

climax.text: Choosing what to grow where, based on water availability, could save trillions of liters globally.

punchline.text: Every crop carries invisible water. Some carry far too much.

quiz.question: How much water does it take to produce one kilogram of beef?

details.summary: A crop's water footprint measures the total freshwater consumed throughout its growth cycle, including rain, irrigation, and water needed to dilute pollutants. This topic covers how water footprints vary by crop, region, and farming practice.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding crop water footprints helps farmers and policymakers decide what to grow where. Growing water-intensive crops in water-scarce regions is increasingly unsustainable.
takeaways: Rice has one of the highest water footprints at roughly 1,700 liters per kilogram
Green water (rain) dominates footprints in rain-fed farming; blue water (irrigation) in arid zones
Improving irrigation efficiency directly reduces the blue water footprint of crops

faq.question: What is a crop water footprint?
faq.answer: It is the total volume of freshwater used to produce a crop, including green water (rain absorbed by soil), blue water (irrigation from rivers or aquifers), and grey water (freshwater needed to dilute production-related pollutants to safe levels).

faq.question: Which crops have the highest and lowest water footprints?
faq.answer: Rice, cotton, and sugarcane have high water footprints (1,500–2,000+ liters per kilogram). Potatoes, carrots, and tomatoes have relatively low footprints (200–300 liters per kilogram). Livestock feed crops compound the footprint of animal products.
